title: Bearman and Gasly reflect on US GP collision
excerpt:
Ollie Bearman and Pierre Gasly have reflected on their collision in the United States Grand Prix, with the former stating "I don't regret going for the move" despite being handed a penalty.

The pair were on the fringes of the top 10 in the early stages of Sunday's race at the Circuit of The Americas, with Bearman having closed up to the Alpine driver as a Virtual Safety Car ended.

Bearman, who had already made up two places on the opening lap, lunged to the inside of Gasly through the right of Turn 13 with the pair making what looked like innocuous contact.

Bearman moved ahead but had suffered extensive damage in the collision, as well as picking up a 10-second penalty for the incident, before the Haas driver eventually retired due to the damage.

"I went up his inside, he saw me because he left space but for me it didn't really feel like enough. It was a bit of space but only half a car and by the time I was committed, I wasn't disappearing," said Bearman.

"So we made a bit of contact, I picked up a huge amount of damage on my car. I probably damaged Pierre's car as well. It was a shame because I felt like I was massively penalised for it and it actually ruined my race to have that amount of damage.

"I was losing a second a lap due to downforce and on top of that, I picked up a penalty. In my view it was a racing incident."

Bearman admitted that he needed to be aggressive as Haas struggle to match the performance of midfield teams such as Alpine and Racing Bulls when fighting for minor points positions.

"To be honest, I don't regret going for the move because at this stage if we don't do something special and get a bit lucky, be a aggressive and go for it, then we're not going to score points because we're not fast enough to do that on merit," added Bearman.

Gasly eventually finished P10, but like Bearman had also suffered damage in the collision which he believes cost him any chance of battling Liam Lawson's Racing Bulls for P9.

"I'm pleased because after the contact with Ollie, we had quite a big damage on the floor," he said.

"It was a small touch honestly and I didn't expect the floor to be that damaged following it. But considering the pace after that and the fact we managed to hold onto P10, it's positive."

He added: "I think [the overtake] was a little optimistic, not crazy, but a little optimistic.

"Unfortunately there was this touch which cost us and cost probably 5-10 seconds of race time following it. It was not ideal, but at the same time, he tried it. It just wasn't the cleanest move."

title: Lawson excited for what’s to come after more points in Austin
excerpt:
Liam Lawson is keen to go racing again at the next two rounds in the latest triple header after securing another points finish at the United States Grand Prix, with the New Zealander feeling in a “good place” following his P9 result.

After lining up as ‘best of the rest’ in ninth place on the grid – behind the Mercedes, Red Bull, Ferrari and McLaren drivers – Lawson put in a solid drive to bring his Racing Bulls machine home in the same position.

The 24-year-old spoke highly of how the team had performed across the event at the Circuit of The Americas, with his result boosting the squad’s tally as their hold on P5 in the Teams’ Championship strengthens.

“When everyone finishes, for us it's a P9 or a P10 – that's sort of the best we can do,” said Lawson. “Honestly we executed really well today – we had a great race, so couldn't really do more. Overall it's been a strong weekend.”

When pushed on how encouraging it is for him personally to see his consistent run continue, Lawson responded: “I mean honestly, yeah. I feel good. I felt good all weekend. I’m enjoying driving this car, honestly – it's in a great place at the moment, so I’m excited to go to some more sort of unique tracks now.

“Obviously with Mexico [it’s] very high altitude, and Brazil [is] probably going to be quite bumpy I'm guessing. But yeah, we're in a good place.”

On the other side of the garage, Arvid Lindblad was faced with a more challenging afternoon on Sunday after a five-place grid penalty for using additional power unit elements dropped him down to P14.

He ultimately went on to cross the line in 12th place, leaving him unsure about how to summarise his race.

“It was okay,” the Briton reflected afterwards. “Lap 1 wasn't as good as I'd hoped – obviously I went down the inside, but we all kind of stacked up on top of each other so I wasn't really able to make any ground there.

“And then it was a bit difficult, the first stint, and then the second two stints I think were okay, but obviously I boxed quite early onto the medium [tyre]. I was feeling good for a few laps – I was catching Franco [Colapinto], and then I was basically in Pierre [Gasly's] undercut window so then he held me up. I lost about two seconds in half a lap with him.

“Then I tried to get Pierre and probably pushed a bit too hard, but yeah, it is what it is. I'm not really sure honestly how to reflect on the race. For half of it I didn't really know where I was or what was going on.

“I think I was the only one who tried to do the two-stop – I don't think that worked. It is what it is. I think there were positives, so we'll learn from it, and yeah, big thanks to the team anyway.”

Despite this, Lindblad was pleased to have felt better in the car than at earlier points of the weekend.

“I didn't feel very comfortable going into [it] through most of the practices, but then I felt okay in Quali,” he explained. “Honestly, I felt pretty good in the race as well – probably one of the best feelings I've had in the race so far this year.”

title: 'More than a bad start' cost Audi after another P11 finish
excerpt:
Nico Hulkenberg finished 11th in Austin as Audi once again came agonisingly close to scoring points. It is the third time in the last four races that the German has come home in P11 – something that has become a theme of Audi’s season as a whole.

The team continue to be in the midfield mix, their last big upgrade package bolted on in Baku propelling them into the fight for points. Despite that however, they have only scored once in the last four Grands Prix – Hulkenberg’s P8 in Singapore delivering four much-needed points to the squad.

Things were always going to be tough at the Circuit of The Americas with Gabriel Bortoleto starting from the back after picking up a raft of penalties for taking on new power unit components, although he should in theory have enough parts in his pool now to make it to the end of the season without further issue.

That left Hulkenberg to fight for points from P11 on the grid, and another poor start made his quest even tougher.

“You can’t call that a bad start, it went into anti-stall so yeah, that’s more than a bad start,” the German said afterwards.

“A strange one as normally the anti-stall kicks in instantly, and I did a few metres and then it kicked in. Sounded and felt a bit odd, but obviously don’t know what happened, [I'm] fresh out of the car so I need to go back and see what happened and why. But of course, it didn’t help our cause for the race.”

Audi have struggled with reliability this season, especially regarding their power unit. As the only team running the Audi PU, they have significantly less data to draw on than the likes of Mercedes and Ferrari, who each supply customer teams.

But while Hulkenberg failed to start two of the first four races, of late the reliability has been much better – Silverstone was the last time he failed to see the chequered flag. But starts remain an issue, with both cars often losing out off the line and leaving them on the back foot.

“You saw again today we were quite close pace-wise with Pierre [Gasly] and with Liam [Lawson], and obviously we came from behind after that start but not sure we could have done a whole lot more from there,” he added.

“It would have all [been] dependent on how with a good start [where] we would have come out, we can only speculate but it is what it is now.”

Audi sit eighth in the Teams' Championship, seven points adrift of Haas in the fight for seventh. While they seem to have the edge on the American team on pace, the opportunities to score are few and far between at the moment.

As for Bortoleto, he enjoyed his afternoon on track, albeit from the back of the field knowing that making it back towards the top 10 would be a tough ask.

“We did a good race, overtook some cars, kept it clean at the same time you know, no damage. I had a bit of fun overtaking people and being out there, trying my best, putting in some good [racing]. Obviously, it is difficult to recover everything starting from the back,” the Brazilian said.

All the key moments from the 2026 United States Grand Prix

He crossed the line 13th, and like his team mate has five P11 results to his name this season. It has been so often the case of close but not close enough for Audi, who have not been helped by Racing Bulls ahead having strong reliability and two drivers in good form.

But all things considered, Audi are enjoying a solid season with the new generation of cars. They have taken the right direction with their upgrades, have an established driver pairing that work well together and have weathered the disruption of Jonathan Wheatley leaving his role as Team Principal.

All of which means the team have a good base from which to launch into 2027, as they try and climb up the order and challenge more consistently for points.

title: Russell struggling with 'difficult' operating window – Wolff
excerpt:
Toto Wolff believes George Russell has struggled to get the most out of Mercedes’ W17 this season due to a “difficult” operating window, with the Briton only finishing eighth in last weekend’s United States Grand Prix.

Russell’s difficult 2026 campaign continued in Austin where he was unable to match race winner Kimi Antonelli, who finished 54 seconds clear of his Mercedes team mate during Sunday's race.

Russell’s race was compromised by serving a five-second penalty during his pit stop due to leaving the track and gaining an advantage, before he became stuck behind Oscar Piastri’s McLaren until the chequered flag.

"George just struggled so much and I believe this is because the operational window of the car is so difficult. In Q2, he was there or thereabouts. Q3 didn't work – he said that goes on me," explained Team Principal Wolff on Sunday.

"And today in the race, I don't know. We got stuck behind Piastri, which looks a bit unfair, why he didn't get past, it's the same engine, it's the same electric charging and deployment."

Antonelli’s ninth win of the season leaves him on the cusp of becoming the youngest driver to claim the title this weekend in Mexico City, having come to grips with the new-for-2026 regulations.

A new package introduced by Mercedes ahead of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia appears to have also widened the gap between himself and Russell, but Wolff is adamant that Russell is still a potential champion.

"I think the update we put on the car is still difficult to operate, and [Kimi] landed it," said Wolff.

"We will try to retrace every decision that we took, and correlate with the lack of performance on Friday and then the relative outperformance Saturday and Sunday. But at least the positive news is that the car works. So now it's about widening the window of operation.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion, and has won in every category, and I think he merits to be put in the group of the very best ones, and we've seen that last year and this year.

"We see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fast. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles, and he struggles more than maybe Kimi.

"And that is on us. We just have to work it out with him, how there can be such a difference in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three-tenths slower than Kimi. It's just absolutely not the case."

title: 5 Winners and 5 Losers from Austin
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli moved to the brink of his first world title with a superb drive in the United States Grand Prix. But as the Italian champion elect celebrated a commanding victory in Austin, others didn’t have much to write home about. Lawrence Barretto selects his winners and losers at the Circuit of The Americas.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli

Mercedes didn’t look like they had a car to challenge for pole position or the race victory based on Friday practice, as the Silver Arrows battled to understand their upgraded 2026-spec car – so it was all the more impressive when Antonelli delivered a stunning lap in Qualifying to claim P1.

title: Stella reflects on McLaren's US GP after missing podium
excerpt:
Andrea Stella believes that McLaren matched the performance of Ferrari and Red Bull during the United States Grand Prix, despite Lando Norris eventually slipping to fifth last weekend.

Norris and McLaren team mate Oscar Piastri struggled in Qualifying ahead of Sunday's race in Austin, the pair only able to achieve eighth and seventh on the grid respectively.

But the potential of the MCL40 briefly appeared for the Grand Prix, at least in the hands of Norris, who was able to run second in the closing stages, before eventually losing out to Max Verstappen's Red Bull, as well as the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.

"I think in the race we saw that what we said could have been the potential of the car was actually realised," said Team Principal Andrea Stella.

"Yesterday [in Qualifying], we thought that we had a faster car than we actually were able to realise on track. Lando said that the car could have been good for P2.

"I think that's a little bit of an exaggeration, because even if the potential was there, this year somehow is very difficult to use the full potential.

“It gets a little bit easier in the race, because you don't push as much as you do in Qualifying. You necessarily leave a little bit of margin, and the car was, I think, today as competitive as the Ferraris and Red Bull, while [Kimi] Antonelli seemed to be a step ahead of everyone else."

Norris was able to move up to second after switching to a one-stop strategy, with Leclerc, Verstappen and Hamilton utilising a two-stop, meaning they were able to hunt down and pass the reigning World Champion towards the end.

Norris believed it was the best result possible, while Piastri was only able to finish seventh having held off Mercedes' George Russell in the process.

"For the one-stop, this gives you the possibility to take advantage of a Safety Car, which didn't come,” said Stella.

"We are still waiting a compensation for what happened in Madrid! It will come, and we also attempted to see what's left in the hard tyres, but honestly, we knew that it was very, very unlikely that we could have kept Verstappen and, in particular, Leclerc behind.

"With Hamilton, we thought it was more dependent on the final tail of the hard tyres."

Since Norris' brace of victories in the summer, the Briton has struggled to come close to achieving similar results, having not finished on the podium in the last four Grands Prix.

Stella confirmed new upgrades would be coming in the next few weeks that would hopefully elevate McLaren back into the fight at the very front of the field.

"There will be some more stuff coming. I think ultimately we will only be able to do so across Brazil and Vegas. So Mexico, there won't be very much, but Brazil and Vegas, there will be some upgrades," said Stella.

"Hopefully, this will help us to, like I said before, be consistently in the fight for podiums and hopefully start to lean on the level of competitiveness that is required to fight for the victory, so there's a few upgrades that are still in the pipeline."

title: Antonelli and Mercedes 'faster than us' in US GP – Mekies
excerpt:
Red Bull's Laurent Mekies admits that Kimi Antonelli and Mercedes were "faster than us" in last weekend's United States Grand Prix, as Max Verstappen could only finish third.

Red Bull entered the event in Austin on the crest of a wave with Verstappen having taken back-to-back wins in Malaysia and Singapore.

The Dutchman started on the front row alongside polesitter Antonelli but failed to challenge the Mercedes driver at the start before Red Bull decided to utilise a two-stop strategy.

With Antonelli and Mercedes sticking to a one-stop, the young Italian was never seriously threatened as he won by 13 seconds from Charles Leclerc, the Ferrari driving having passed Verstappen in the closing stages.

"I think Kimi had more pace than us today. I don't think we can use any excuse of tyres or of strategy. I think Kimi was faster than us today. Fair play, and well done to him," said Team Principal Mekies.

"It's probably fair to say that one-stop and two-stop looks very close in terms of race times. We split our cars, as you have seen. I think Ferrari was on two stops, and I think McLaren was one-stop. So I think in race time, they were probably very, very close.

"It's probably fair to say that we normally enjoy a bit of an advantage compared to competition with the softer compounds, and today we have struggled to use that advantage.

"We have suffered some fairly high deg with Max on the two sets of soft compounds that we had – and that certainly didn't help materialising the second stop."

Red Bull's strategy played out with a new voice over the radio for Verstappen, as Tom Hart filled in the role for regular race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase, who is set to move to McLaren.

How 'everything went wrong' for Red Bull in United States GP

Mekies believes Hart did a great job during a baptism of fire, with he and GP set to alternate the role until the end of the season.

"I think he did an excellent job, and you see me smiling because I certainly remember what it is to be on your first race as a race engineer," said Mekies.

"And he picked a fairly complicated race to do that, but that was not his choice! But joke aside, I think he really did an excellent job.

"First Qualifying, first race, he has managed to channel very well the work of the engineering teams behind him to Max. And of course the race was a complicated race, and we are probably a bit frustrated with the P3, which is the good news.

"But I really think he did an excellent job, and he was very well supported by GP as well in the background. You cannot recreate a relationship in no time. But I have every confidence that we are going to see him ramping up and building that relationship with Max."

One area of improvement that Mekies is keen to see is in regards to Red Bull's starts, with both Verstappen and team mate Isack Hadjar, who finished sixth, losing positions on the opening lap due to poor launches and sub-optimal battery deployment.

"As much as we have reduced the gap to competition, and you may remember how bad our starts were at the beginning of the year, we are still not the benchmark,” he said.

"And yes, the fact that the car in the meantime improved a lot and is fighting closer to the front makes that deficit even more painful now, because competition around us is very strong.

"On one side, I'm confident that we will continue to reduce the gap to the competition from now to the end of the year, because every race we learn, every race we come up with small ways to close the gap.

"On the other side, I equally know that we will not be the benchmark before the end of the season, that it will require some significant design and hardware changes, and that this is something that we will see only next year."

title: Williams protege gets latest F1 practice outing in double swap
excerpt:
Williams has confirmed that protege Luke Browning is to get a further two FP1 outings in 2026 - starting at the Mexico City Grand Prix this weekend.

Browning, who has already driven the FW48 in Barcelona, Austria, and Italy, will take five total FP1s this season, as he takes over Alex Albon's car in Mexico before Carlos Sainz steps down for FP1 in Brazil.

Browning's first FP1 of the year in Barcelona was ruined by car problems, meaning he conducted no meaningful running - with Albon, who stepped aside in Italy for the second time, now giving up a third session for the Briton.

Other FP1 drivers confirmed thus far are Fred Vesti for George Russell at Mercedes, Jak Crawford for Lance Stroll at Aston Martin and Freddie Slater for Audi, although it has not been confirmed which driver Slater will replace in Mexico when he makes his debut, but it is likely to be Gabriel Bortoleto.

Slater is also in for FP1 in Brazil, with this being Bortoleto's home race, meaning Nico Hulkenberg should likely stand down there.

title: Isack Hadjar demands Red Bull fixes 'stupid little things' ruining F1 races
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has demanded that Red Bull find fixes for "stupid little things" which impacted his United States GP after a mixed weekend.

After a poor Friday, which he branded a "disaster" as he struggled for balance and feeling in the RB22, Hadjar rebounded to qualify in third place for the grand prix, 0.036s behind team-mate Max Verstappen in second.

In the race, a poor launch for Hadjar dropped him behind both Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, with the French racer also dropping behind Lando Norris's McLaren in the final results for a sixth-place finish.

His efforts were enough to see Red Bull leapfrog McLaren into third place in the constructors, with the two teams level on points, with Red Bull ahead on countback with four second places to McLaren's two, as both have 355 points and two grand prix wins apiece.

However, when asked for his reflections on the up-and-down Austin weekend, after his struggles on Friday and then third in qualifying, Hadjar declared that the team must "nail" the "stupid little things."

"Friday was a total mess, and my race pace was not good, and we turned some things around in FP3 and in qualifying, we had a good car," he began to media, including RacingNews365.

"The race pace [on Sunday] was good, and the hard part of it, we nailed, but the little stupid things, the little details, we need to nail them as well."

Adding further detail on these areas, Hadjar pinpointed the ongoing radio issues both cars are suffering from and the long-standing clutch and start problems.

"At the moment, it is the little things we can't do," he said.

"I have a poor radio; I don't even know what is happening. I drop the clutch, and it is a nightmare, so if we fix these two [issues], we might be on the podium.

"It is the hardest things it seems like we can do, and the silly things we can't."

[Article continues below]

Stuck in the wrong mode

Hadjar also revealed that following his pit-stop and move to the hard tyres, his RB22 machine became stuck in the wrong engine mode - something that was unable to be changed once he rejoined the race.

"Exiting the pits, I was stuck in the pit-stop throttle map, and you don't want to drive like that," he said.

"The pace on the hard was pretty good, but I was stuck with the pit-stop throttle map and from the second lap already, this was the issue.

"Honestly, what tyres [I had on] was the least of my issues, and I had a drivability problem, and then you can put the wet tyres on, and it is not going to change anything."

title: Honda declare upgrade 'roadmap' for big Aston Martin F1 boost
excerpt:
Honda has explained that it is targeting two big F1 upgrades for the 2027 season to bring a major boost to Aston Martin.

The new alliance has struggled with performance and reliability in 2026, with issues including a lack of power, severe vibrations, turbo lag, and drivability concerns.

Under the ADUO mechanism, Honda will be granted two upgrades for 2027 to allow it to try and catch up with other manufacturers; in a year, the power unit will be slightly tweaked to bring out more internal combustion power to reduce reliance on the battery systems.

Combustion is an area the engine has also struggled with, but chief engineer Shintaro Orihara is optimistic that twin upgrades, including one mid-2027, can bring the Japanese manufacturer, and thus Aston Martin, into line with its rivals.

"We need some steps to catch up to the top competitors, and our target is to bring some steps for round one [of 2027]," Orihara told media, including RacingNews365.

"But still, at round one, we can say we wouldn't be a top competitor, so we need one more step.

"So, as Adrian [Newey] has said, our target is to take another big step in the middle of the season, let's say maybe round eight [in Monaco].

"That is our roadmap, and we are working based on that roadmap.

"Our weak point is combustion, so we're working hard to improve our combustion, especially for next year, when [ICE] performance is more important compared to this year, so that is a key point for us."

[Article continues below]

Aston Martin back Honda

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack was then asked about the team potentially exploring a Red Bull Powertrains deal for 2028, should it decide to split from Honda.

However, he rejected the idea.

"I can only say that we have a partner, a long-term partner, which is Honda," he said.

"Which, by the way, has done its 500th race [in Austin], and I think we will be together when we win our first race together."

title: George Russell to miss crucial Mexico GP session in mandatory F1 absence
excerpt:
George Russell will miss Free Practice 1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix, as team-mate Kimi Antonelli is on the cusp of the title.

For the first time in 2026, Russell will step out of the W17 for one of the two mandatory sessions he must give to a young driver - with Mercedes reserve Fred Vesti stepping into Russell's cockpit at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Antonelli had missed FP1 at the Barcelona-Catalunya and Hungarian Grands Prix earlier in the season to fulfil his two slots in favour of Vesti with Russell now required to miss one more session this year.

Mexico, owing to the dusty track conditions found in FP1, is a common place for drivers to miss one of their sessions and hand over to the younger driver before returning for FP2.

Russell must win the grand prix this weekend to have any hopes of beating Antonelli to the title, with the Italian holding a 123-point lead over the Briton, with 125 points remaining.

If Russell does not win, Antonelli will win the title by default, with Antonelli requiring a ninth-place finish if Russell does claim victory.

Lewis Hamilton also remains in contention, and if he also does not win, Antonelli is champion - with a 10th place sufficing should the seven-time champion win the race.

Vesti is not the only FP1 driver confirmed for Mexico thus far, with Aston Martin giving Jak Crawford a latest run-out, whilst Audi is to hand protege Freddie Slater his F1 weekend debut with his first FP1.

title: Red Bull explain 'painful' issue that will not be fixed until next F1 season
excerpt:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has confirmed that the clutch problems plaguing the RB22 will not be resolved until next season, after Isack Hadjar called for a redesign following the United States Grand Prix.

Hadjar finished sixth at the Circuit of the Americas, but said after the race that the car's clutch assembly is "fragile" and struggles with operating temperatures, with start issues occurring that were not down to driver error.

Red Bull has endured launch problems throughout this campaign, with Max Verstappen and Hadjar regularly losing ground off the line compared to the frontrunners at Ferrari, McLaren and Mercedes.

Speaking about the launch issues, Mekies said the problem touches almost every department at the team.

"The start is a slightly more complex issue to solve," said Mekies, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365.

"The staff performance is going across pretty much all of the departments of the company, probably except aerodynamics. It's the engine, it's the gearbox, it's the clutch, it's many things.

"We have seen from the beginning of the season that we are not the benchmark in terms of launch performance. As much as we have reduced the gap to the competition, and you may remember how bad our starts were at the beginning of the year, we are still not the benchmark.

"The fact that the car in the meantime has improved a lot and is fighting closer to the front makes that deficit even more painful now because the competition around us is very strong.

"So, on one side, I'm confident that we will continue to reduce the gap to the competition from now to the end of the year because every race we learn, and every race we come up with small ways to close the gap.

"On the other side, I equally know that we will not be the benchmark before the end of the season, that it will require some significant design and hardware changes, and that this is something that we will only see next year."

[Article continues below]

Mekies - 'Truth in what Isack is saying'

Red Bull's weekend in Austin was also compromised by a separate problem: recurring radio dropouts that left Max Verstappen and Hadjar without pit instructions on occasion.

It marked the second consecutive race in which Red Bull's radio system had failed its drivers mid-session.

Mekies conceded that Hadjar's frustration, in particular, over the communication failures was justified.

"There is some truth in what Isack is saying, meaning we are all frustrated to struggle for the second race in a row with the radio issues," said Mekies. "It's making everyone's lives very difficult.

"It is true that it's something that we would like to fix quite quickly because it's an item that should be working without using too much of our energy, so he's right on that one.

"And if we understood it, we would have solved it, but we don't fully understand why we are being hit by these issues.

"I have to admit that the competition is doing a better job than us because we can obviously hear everyone's radio, and we have been struggling more than we would have liked to."

title: Carlos Sainz stunned by Arvid Lindblad penalty escape: 'Pretty nasty moment'
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has expressed surprise that Arvid Lindblad escaped a penalty for squeezing him against the pit wall at the start of the United States Grand Prix.

Fast-starting Williams driver Sainz tried to force his way through when faced with Lindblad's Racing Bulls ahead of him, only for the British driver to close the door on the Spaniard along the front straight, leading to him kissing the wall.

Sainz avoided serious contact but picked up front-wing damage in the process, which compromised his opening stint. The Spaniard was eventually forced to pit for a new nose that cost him several seconds, before recovering to finish 18th, one lap down.

Despite the severity of the squeeze, no investigation was opened, and Lindblad was not penalised by the stewards for the clash.

Speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Sainz said his own race had started well before the incident unfolded.

"It was a good start," said Sainz. "We've picked up a trend now where I think everyone knows we're getting very good starts, and they kind of put us off a bit at the start always.

"I'm surprised he [Lindblad] got away with that because, obviously, he's putting someone in the wall and creating what could have potentially been a very big accident.

"I backed out in time, but I picked up a lot of front-wing damage, which compromised my first stint. On top of that, obviously a slow pit stop to change the front wing, seven, eight seconds extra, but then I managed to recover from there, and I settled down into a decent pace for the rest of the race.

"So yeah, bit of a shame at the start and that lap one was compromised, and stint one was compromised, but it is what it is."

[Article continues below]

Sainz - 'I've never got away with it'

The Williams driver went further when reflecting on the lack of sanction, questioning why the same standard did not appear to apply to him when he has been judged too aggressive in the past.

"We are all very high standards," said Sainz. "It's just that sometimes someone has a bit of an off moment, which always happens in F1.

"My opinion is that Arvid was maybe too much on me, but we've all been too much one or two days.

"What I'm surprised is that when you're too much, you get away with it. Whenever I've been too much, I've never got away with it.

"I'm surprised that someone got away with it because it was a pretty nasty moment there on the wall."

title: Just how rich Is Max Verstappen? — Here's how much Verstappen will earn in 2026
excerpt:
Max Verstappen is raking it in in Formula 1, and he has once again climbed significantly in the list of the richest Dutch people in the Quote 500 this year.

With an estimated net worth of 310 million euros, he has climbed to 224th place on the list. Last year, he was ranked 264th with an estimated net worth of 260 million euros.

Max Verstappen earns about 70 million euros annually in Formula 1, making him the highest-paid driver, followed by Lewis Hamilton with about 54 million euros annually.

The Quote 500 is published annually and has a new leader this year with crypto mogul Jean-Louis van der Velde, who has an estimated net worth of 26 billion euros.

Van der Velde thus dethrones Charlene de Carvalho-Heineken, daughter of Heineken founder Freddy Heineken, who still holds a respectable second place with an estimated net worth of 13 billion euros.

title: Toto Wolff explains why Mercedes must 'work' with George Russell
excerpt:
Toto Wolff plans for Mercedes to work specifically with George Russell to help close the performance gap that has emerged between the British driver and team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Toto Wolff has vehemently come to the defence of George Russell, who has endured an unexpectedly underwhelming and inconsistent F1 season.

Coming into the campaign, Russell was the bookmakers' favourite for the drivers' championship, and many anticipated that he would ease his way to his first title.

Not only has that not happened, but it has been Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli who has cruised to the crown, with the 20-year-old almost certainly going to be coronated at the upcoming Mexico City Grand Prix.

Despite the bitterly disappointing year for Russell, Wolff insists the British driver is one of the "very best" in Formula 1, even if he has fallen short of expectations.

"George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category," the Mercedes team principal told media, including RacingNews365.

"And I think he merits being put in the group of the very best ones — we've seen that last year.

"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fast.

"But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles; and he struggles more than maybe Kimi."

[Article continues below]

Driver

George Russell

British

63

Russell slower than Antonelli?

Put plainly, Russell has too often been unable to extract the same level of performance from the W17 as Antonelli.

Whilst dominant on his day, too frequently the eight-time grand prix winner has had to play second fiddle to his team-mate, on top of experiencing more than his fair share of bad luck and reliability issues.

Further reflecting on the disparity in pace — not only between his two drivers, but also from when the car is performing as hoped and when it is outside of its ideal window — Wolff revealed Mercedes would work with Russell to close the delta to Antonelli.

"That is on us," the Austrian explained. "We just have to work it out with him on how there can be such a difference in performance, because George is not half a second slower, [or] three tenths slower than Kimi. It's just absolutely not the case.

"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast, because it's all there in intelligence, the ability, the determination."

title: The question supporting newest Formula E team principal: 'What would Frank do?'
excerpt:
The new Fortescue Zero Racing Formula E outfit has Williams F1 running through its veins, but also in how it will operate.

Jim Wright has revealed the guiding principle behind his new role as team principal of Fortescue Zero Racing: asking himself what Sir Frank Williams would have done in his position.

Wright was confirmed as team boss of the newly formed Formula E outfit after Fortescue Zero bought out the Penske Autosport operation in September, with the squad set to compete under the Fortescue Zero Racing name from the start of the Gen4 era in the 2026/27 campaign.

The motorsport veteran has spent decades in the paddock, including more than 10 years at Williams F1 between 1994 and 2006, where he rose from leading sponsorship sales to head of marketing and a seat on the team's management board, working directly under Sir Frank Williams and Patrick Head.

Speaking to RacingNews365 about why now felt like the right moment to step into the top job, Wright pointed to that grounding alongside one of the sport's most respected figures.

"I've been in motorsport all my life," began telling Wright. "I'm a very lucky guy, and I've learned from some true icons of the sport, like Frank Williams, being alongside him, so I think the time is right.

"I feel ready to take on this role. I've got experience, and I've been in Formula E, working alongside all of the team principals in my FETAMA role, which I had for 10 years.

"So I know Formula E inside out. I know what good looks like. I know what mediocre looks like. I know what bad looks like.

"And it's my job now to make sure that we create something which is really, really good, and that Fortescue can be really proud of."

The Williams DNA within Fortescue Zero Racing

Wright's decade coordinating the Formula E Teams and Manufacturers Association (FETAMA) gave him a unique vantage point inside the paddock, working across rival garages to align teams and manufacturers on governance, sporting regulations and the technical roadmaps that shaped the Gen3 era and now Gen4.

That experience followed earlier commercial roles at Venturi, Mahindra and Andretti, on top of his formative years at Williams and spells with Toro Rosso and Virgin Racing/Marussia.

Fortescue Zero itself carries Williams heritage. The outfit traces its lineage directly to Williams Advanced Engineering, the technology arm founded by Williams F1, which was bought by Fortescue in 2022 and later rebranded.

The business had already supplied the spec battery packs for Formula E's Gen1 and Gen3 cars as well as the PitBoost system before Fortescue Zero's move to become a full works entrant powered by Jaguar.

Asked what his leadership style will look like, Wright explained: "I'm trying consciously, with every big decision, to think, 'What would Frank do here?' And Frank was a huge inspiration to me, certainly a mentor, and I learned a lot from the way he approached things, and Patrick Head as well.

"I was fortunate enough to work alongside both of them. So I think my approach to big decision-making will be: let's look at this from all angles.

"Let's be calm, reasoned, and ask, 'What would Frank do?' So that is going to be my approach."

title: Lando Norris hands McLaren brutal 'nowhere' verdict: 'We need a lot more'
excerpt:
Lando Norris has delivered a damning assessment of McLaren's upgrade package after the United States Grand Prix, declaring the team is "nowhere near the level we need to be at" in slow-speed corners.

Norris finished fifth at Circuit of the Americas, having been promoted ahead of team-mate Oscar Piastri during the race.

The Briton explained that the swap was straightforward given his pace advantage over the Australian that weekend.

Discussing being let past Piastri, Norris told select media, including RacingNews365: "Yeah, I mean, we want the best result. So, I've been a lot quicker all weekend, so it's just the obvious thing to do."

McLaren brought a new package to Austin featuring revised brakes and experimental floor modifications, the latter understood to be early evaluation work for the team's 2027 car concept.

The Woking-based squad remained fourth in the constructors' standings behind Mercedes, Ferrari and Red Bull, with McLaren level on points with the Milton Keynes outfit but behind on countback.

Lando Norris outlines clear McLaren weakness

Asked whether the upgrades delivered as expected, Norris gave a detailed breakdown of where the package had, and had not, moved the needle.

"Yeah, you just hope that you put something on and it's magical, and you go a lot quicker and you're fighting for a podium all of a sudden," said Norris.

"Things are all working as they should, but other teams, Ferrari brought upgrades, and other teams are still bringing in upgrades. So, they're delivering; it's just not, I guess, just not really in all the places that we need them to."

"Like the slow-speed corners, we're just nowhere near the level we need to be at. We need a lot more, a lot more rear and slow speed.

"It's been our issue for a long time now. It seems to be very hard to tackle, but we'll keep working."

Norris's comments point to a weakness that has dogged the MCL40 across the season, with slow-speed corner rotation and rear-end stability flagged repeatedly as persistent traits in the car's characteristics.

McLaren is expected to continue introducing further developments through the remaining rounds of the campaign, with another step planned ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

title: Charles Leclerc explains stunning Max Verstappen overtake after 'coming to play'
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has talked through his stunning first-lap overtake on Max Verstappen in a United States Grand Prix where there was "something to play for."

Although Ferrari's practice pace did not translate into a strong qualifying, with Leclerc fourth and Lewis Hamilton fifth, Leclerc quickly passed both Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar on the opening lap, with Hamilton also dispatching Hadjar and having a go at Verstappen.

Slow away, Verstappen was passed around the outside of Turns 4 and 5 by Leclerc, who squeaked through, before Verstappen sliced back past later in the lap to regain second place.

As the two engaged in a two-stop strategy duel, the race boiled down to a fight for second place in the closing stages, with Leclerc getting ahead of his rival at Turn 12 to pick up the runner-up trophy behind runaway leader Kimi Antonelli.

Reflecting, Leclerc spoke of how he managed to pass Verstappen on the opening lap as he realised there was "something to play for".

"That was fun. I mean, I had quite a good start, and then I didn't want to brake too late for Turn 1, just to keep an opportunity of trying to cross back at the exit of Turn 1," Leclerc told media, including RacingNews365.

"But Lewis got very, very close, and then I used a little bit more of my battery to get alongside Max in Turns 3, 4, and 5.

"I didn't really know how it would go, but it was quite close, and it was fun.

"I enjoyed [the race]. I mean, the start was fun, then later on with Lando and Max again was quite fun. So, it's one of those races where you're not getting too bored inside the cockpit, and there's something to play for.

"I even thought the victory was possible at one point when I saw Kimi going for the one-stop. Based on our numbers, he would start to struggle a bit more towards the end of the race.

“He never really struggled towards the end of the race, but, it was a fun race. It is a shame just that we came short of winning."

[Article continues below].

Leclerc agrees with Ferrari strategy

As for his strategy, Leclerc felt that the two-stop was the correct way to go, but that he just did not have the pace to defeat the one-stopping Antonelli, who finished 13s up the road.

"I think Red Bull and I had kind of the same vision. If you look at the tyre allocation as well, for us the two-stops were probably the way to go," Leclerc added.

"The hard was just a really good tyre, and I could push on it quite a lot. So, yeah, I was more interested in trying to... I kept asking my engineer what the pace of Kimi was, but I was probably a bit too optimistic.

"I still wanted to give it a shot, but I probably lost a bit too much time with Max and Lando, and even with free air, I don't think I would have got to Kimi."

title: Red Bull promise 'review' after Max Verstappen strategy complaint
excerpt:
Max Verstappen said his soft-soft-medium tyre strategy for the United States GP was not what was agreed beforehand. Laurent Mekies, however, doubts any strategy would have beaten Kimi Antonelli.

Red Bull will "review" why Max Verstappen's strategy at the United States Grand Prix led to higher-than-expected tyre degradation after the Dutchman questioned the approach taken in Austin.

Verstappen finished third at the Circuit of the Americas, 17.485 seconds behind race winner Kimi Antonelli, after Red Bull ran him on a soft-soft-medium strategy. Antonelli's medium-to-hard one-stop proved to be the pace-setting approach for the Mercedes driver.

The four-time F1 champion suggested after the race that the strategy did not match what had been agreed beforehand, though Mekies said he had not heard the specific comments.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Mekies said: "I'm not sure what he was referring to because I didn't hear what he said.

"But I think one thing that may have surprised him is the fact that we elected to put him on the soft for the second stint, which was the baseline option for us.

"Unfortunately, as you may have seen in that second stint, we suffered fairly high degradation. So it is probably one of the things we will review together on why we degraded that much in that second stint."

[Article continues below]

Mekies - 'We struggled to use that advantage'

Red Bull split its strategies between Verstappen and team-mate Isack Hadjar, who crossed the line sixth, but Mekies insisted the choice of tyres or strategy had little bearing on the result against Antonelli.

"I think Kimi had more pace than us," said Mekies. "I don't think we can use any excuse of tyres or of strategy. Kimi was faster. Fair play and well done to him.

"It's probably fair to say that one-stop and two-stop were very close in terms of race times. We split our cars, as you saw.

"It's also probably fair to say that we normally enjoy a bit of an advantage compared to the competition with the softer compounds, and we struggled to use that advantage.

"We suffered some fairly high deg with Max on the two sets of soft compounds that we had, and that certainly didn't help."

title: Lewis Hamilton spies costly issue Ferrari must 'get on top of'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton encountered a problem during the United States Grand Prix that he feels robbed him of a better finishing position.

Lewis Hamilton has identified a persistent balance issue with his Ferrari that he believes is preventing him from achieving stronger results, insisting there is considerably more performance to unlock if the problem can be resolved.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion finished fourth in the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas, behind team-mate Charles Leclerc, who secured second place.

However, Hamilton was left frustrated by the performance of his SF-26, having struggled with significant understeer during the opening two stints of the race, which compromised his ability to challenge Max Verstappen for the final podium position.

The 41-year-old revealed that his difficulties stemmed from an incorrect set-up direction during Friday practice, with Ferrari subsequently making adjustments that left him closer to Leclerc's configuration by the final session.

Despite those changes, Hamilton started the race with less front wing than his team-mate, leaving him unable to turn the car as effectively as required.

The Briton explained that Ferrari added four clicks of front wing at each of his two pit stops, but even after those adjustments, he felt he remained another four clicks short of the balance he needed.

Hamilton consequently enjoyed a considerably stronger final stint, leaving him convinced that a better starting set-up would have allowed him to fight for a podium.

The Ferrari driver believes addressing the recurring issue will be crucial to maximising his results over the remaining rounds of the campaign.

"There's lots of positives to take from it," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365. "I think lots of learnings. I think for the next races, if I can really get on top of this balance issue that I have, I think we can get much better results.

"I think if I had had the balance that I need... even if I just had the balancing of the last stint, I would have been, I would have right in the fight all the way to the end. Even then, another step from there, I think we should have probably qualified better. So some good pointers."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Lewis Hamilton

British

44

Hamilton reflects on ill-fated Ferrari tyre decision

In addition to the balance difficulties, Hamilton highlighted a tyre allocation decision that he believes further compromised his chances of a stronger result in Austin.

Ferrari had opted to retain two sets of medium tyres for the Briton, anticipating that the hard compound would not be particularly effective during the race.

However, the hard ultimately proved to be the strongest race tyre, leaving Hamilton to question whether a different allocation would have offered greater flexibility.

The decision also contributed to Hamilton starting the grand prix on a used set of soft tyres, putting him at a disadvantage compared to the drivers immediately ahead, who had fresh rubber available.

Despite the difference, Hamilton made a strong getaway and came close to moving into third place, although Leclerc's positioning on the outside prevented him from capitalising on the opportunity.

Reflecting on the decision, Hamilton acknowledged that Ferrari's expectations surrounding the tyre compounds had proved incorrect.

"I chose to have two medium tyres because we didn't think the hard tyre was going to be any good," Hamilton said. "In hindsight, two hard tyres would have been the better one. The hard tyre was the best tyre.

"And then it meant I started on a used soft, which — from used to new — is two seconds of race time, and it affects the start as well compared to others that are on new [tyres].

"All the cars ahead were on new, but I had a really good start. Nearly got to third place, but Charles was on the outside, and I didn't get to capitalise on that."

title: Max Verstappen ends remarkable F1 streak with failure to win in Austin
excerpt:
Max Verstappen was unable to take victory in the United States Grand Prix from second on the grid, tumbling out of F1 drivers' championship contention, as Kimi Antonelli triumphed from pole.

Verstappen needed to win at the Circuit of the Americas to stand any chance of clinching a fifth title, although realistically, his hopes never really began in earnest this season.

Nonetheless, he remained in contention, in large part due to his recent flourish, with wins in Sepang and Singapore.

However, the result in Austin means the Red Bull driver is out of the F1 drivers' championship fight for the first time since 2020, when he fell out of contention after the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix, with four subsequent rounds remaining.

That ends a streak of 2,184 days, just shy of six whole years, such has been the Dutchman's dominance of F1 over that period.

Although it does pale in comparison to the run Verstappen's old adversary Lewis Hamilton went on between the Japanese Grand Prix in 2013, his first season at Mercedes and the Italian Grand Prix in 2022.

That record covered 179 races and 3,256 days, and is the longest run between falling out of title contention in F1 history.

Michael Schumacher would likely have held the record, had it not been for breaking his leg at Silverstone in 1999.

If that did not come to pass, it is reasonable to assume he would have either won the title that year or at least pushed Mika Hakkinen all the way.

In that hypothetical, his run would have started when he surrendered his crown at the Hungarian Grand Prix in 1996 and continued until the Italian Grand Prix in 2005 — a timespan of 3,311 days.
